---
title: "Data-generating processes"
---

The event-structure annotations in [Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS)](https://aclanthology.org/2020.lrec-1.699/) attach properties to predicate nodes anchored in sentence context. In the natural-parts task, an annotator first reports whether the situation described by a predicate has natural subparts. The response is evidence about event structure under this instrument; it is not event structure itself. [Gantt, Glass, and White (2022)](https://aclanthology.org/2022.tacl-1.2/) describe the event protocol and its conditional branches, while the [Decomp documentation](https://decomp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/data/semantic-types.html) describes the released semantic graph attributes.

A **data-generating process (DGP)** is an ordered account of the random choices and
deterministic mappings that could produce an observation. We begin with the observed
binary gate because the local extract contains its raw responses. We could not
reconcile the available conditional follow-up and confidence fields with the
documented response scales, so this analysis does not invent those responses.

Recall that an [expected value](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) is an average under a probability model, while [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) licenses multiplication of joint probabilities. The DGP below declares independence only for raw latent coordinates and then shows how shared centered effects induce dependence among response rows.

We inspect the measurement record, trace the observed response process, write its
random steps one at a time, and then use one released item to mark the boundary of
the supported DGP.

## What a UDS row records {#uds-data}

The item is a predicate node in sentence context. Item `ewt-test-963%%ewt-test-963-semantics-pred-6` anchors *exhibited* in “His artworks were selected and exhibited in British Museum in 2002.” The mapping uses the [`decomp` graph-ID convention](https://decomp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/data/syntactic-graphs.html) and the [UD English EWT 1.2 test sentence](https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/UD_English-EWT/blob/r1.2/en-ud-test.conllu). An annotator answers whether the event described by the highlighted predicate has natural subparts. The local `natural_parts` field codes no as 0 and yes as 1.

The full protocol branches after that gate. A yes response reveals questions about
similarity among the parts and their typical duration; a no response reveals
questions about dynamicity and whole-event duration. Duration uses ordered anchors
ranging from effectively no time through seconds, minutes, longer calendar units,
and effectively forever. We could not verify raw fields for those branch responses
in this extract. The empirical model on this page thus concerns only the binary gate,
while [gated annotations](gated-annotations.qmd#the-observed-protocol) returns to the
full symbolic protocol.

## Inspecting the observed response process

```{r}
#| label: load-uds-generative
#| message: false
#| warning: false

uds <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/uds/uds-natural-parts.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(uds) == 2955L,
  length(unique(uds$item_id)) == 1000L,
  length(unique(uds$annotator_id)) == 12L,
  setequal(unique(uds$natural_parts), 0:1),
  sum(uds$natural_parts) == 659L,
  !anyDuplicated(paste(uds$item_id, uds$annotator_id, sep = "::")),
  all(uds$item_id == paste(uds$graph_id, uds$node_id, sep = "%%"))
)

item_response_counts <- table(uds$item_id)
response_summary <- data.frame(
  responses = nrow(uds),
  items = length(unique(uds$item_id)),
  annotators = length(unique(uds$annotator_id)),
  no = sum(uds$natural_parts == 0L),
  yes = sum(uds$natural_parts == 1L),
  items_with_two_responses = sum(item_response_counts == 2L),
  items_with_three_responses = sum(item_response_counts == 3L)
)

knitr::kable(response_summary)

uds[uds$item_id == "ewt-test-963%%ewt-test-963-semantics-pred-6",
    c("split", "graph_id", "node_id", "annotator_id", "natural_parts")]
```

The extract contains `r format(response_summary$responses, big.mark = ",")` responses to `r format(response_summary$items, big.mark = ",")` predicate nodes from `r response_summary$annotators` anonymized annotators. Of these responses, `r response_summary$yes` are yes and `r response_summary$no` are no. The item identifier joins a graph identifier to a predicate-node identifier; it is not a verb lemma.

The annotation design is sparse and crossed. The raw rates below describe the responses each annotator happened to give to the items they saw. They do not yet separate annotator response location from item composition.

```{r}
#| label: plot-uds-annotator-design
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Raw natural-parts response rates by anonymized annotator. Point size records the number of observed responses."

annotator_n <- stats::aggregate(natural_parts ~ annotator_id, uds, length)
names(annotator_n)[2] <- "responses"
annotator_rate <- stats::aggregate(natural_parts ~ annotator_id, uds, mean)
names(annotator_rate)[2] <- "yes_rate"
annotator_design <- merge(annotator_n, annotator_rate, by = "annotator_id")
annotator_design$annotator_id <- stats::reorder(
  annotator_design$annotator_id,
  annotator_design$yes_rate
)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  annotator_design,
  ggplot2::aes(yes_rate, annotator_id, size = responses)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(color = "steelblue4", alpha = 0.85) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 6), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Raw natural-parts yes rate",
    y = "Anonymized annotator"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

## Stating one step at a time

Let $i$ index predicate nodes and $j$ index annotators. The fitted model uses centered raw deviations, so its data-generating process has six steps.

1. Draw independent raw item coordinates $z_i^{\text{item}}$ from a standard normal distribution.
2. Subtract their realized mean and multiply by $\sigma_{\text{item}}$ to construct zero-sum item deviations $u_i$.
3. Draw independent raw annotator coordinates $z_j^{\text{annotator}}$ and apply the analogous transformation to construct $a_j$.
4. Draw the population location $\alpha$ and the two positive raw-deviation scales from their stated priors.
5. Map the population location and centered deviations to a yes probability $\pi_{ij}$.
6. Draw the recorded response $Y_{ij}$ from that probability.

The corresponding model is

$$
z_i^{\text{item}}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1),
\qquad
u_i
=\sigma_{\text{item}}
\left(z_i^{\text{item}}-\bar z^{\text{item}}\right),
$$

$$
z_j^{\text{annotator}}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,1),
\qquad
a_j
=\sigma_{\text{annotator}}
\left(z_j^{\text{annotator}}-\bar z^{\text{annotator}}\right),
$$

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_{ij})=\alpha+u_i+a_j,
\qquad
Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij}).
$$

The dependence sequence is

$$
(\mathbf z^{\text{item}},\mathbf z^{\text{annotator}},
\sigma_{\text{item}},\sigma_{\text{annotator}},\alpha)
\longrightarrow
(\mathbf u,\mathbf a)
\longrightarrow\pi_{ij}\longrightarrow Y_{ij}.
$$

The arrows describe an order of generation, not a chronology in the annotator's mind. The response is the only observed quantity in this sequence. The probability and both deviations are model quantities.

The centered effects sum to zero but are not mutually independent. With $I$ items,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[u_i]
=\sigma_{\text{item}}^2\left(1-\frac{1}{I}\right),
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}[u_i,u_{i'}]
=-\frac{\sigma_{\text{item}}^2}{I}
\quad(i\ne i'),
$$

and the annotator effects have the analogous formulas with $J$. Thus $\sigma_{\text{item}}$ and $\sigma_{\text{annotator}}$ are scales for the raw standard-normal deviations before centering. The marginal standard deviation of a realized centered effect is smaller by the factor $\sqrt{1-1/I}$ or $\sqrt{1-1/J}$.

Each choice encodes a substantive assumption. Bernoulli sampling matches one binary gate response. The logit link keeps $\pi_{ij}$ in $(0,1)$ while allowing item and annotator contributions to add on the log-odds scale. Independent raw normal coordinates produce exchangeable, symmetric, light-tailed centered vectors, while their deterministic centering fixes a finite-sample origin. Additivity assumes no item--annotator interaction beyond those two locations. Finally, responses are conditionally independent given $u_i$, $a_j$, and $\alpha$; marginally, rows sharing an item or annotator remain dependent.

These assumptions may fail. A few annotators might use the gate in qualitatively
different ways, item difficulty might have heavy tails, or particular annotators
might react differently to particular event types. A later
[posterior predictive check](../statistical-inference/posterior-predictive-checks.qmd)
will draw replicated response tables under parameter values from the posterior and
compare their summaries with the observed table. Such checks can expose some
consequences of failed assumptions, but they cannot prove the latent decomposition
uniquely correct.

The observed/model ledger is thus:

| Quantity | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $Y_{ij}$ | observed for $(i,j)\in\mathcal O$ | recorded no/yes gate response |
| item and annotator IDs | observed design | which effects are shared across rows |
| $\pi_{ij}$ | model-implied | conditional yes probability |
| $u_i,a_j$ | latent | item and annotator log-odds deviations |
| $\alpha,\sigma_{\text{item}},\sigma_{\text{annotator}}$ | unknown parameters | population location and variation |

## Grounding the indices in an observed item

The following code chooses the first predicate node in file order that received both response values and prints its recorded rows. Selection depends on response pattern here only to make disagreement visible; it is not part of the prepared extract's construction or any fitted model.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-uds-item

responses_by_item <- split(uds$natural_parts, uds$item_id)
mixed_item_ids <- names(responses_by_item)[
  vapply(responses_by_item, function(x) length(unique(x)) == 2L, logical(1))
]
example_item <- uds[
  uds$item_id == mixed_item_ids[[1]],
  c("split", "graph_id", "node_id", "annotator_id", "natural_parts")
]

knitr::kable(example_item)
```

These rows share one $u_i$ but have different annotator indices $j$. A joint model may attribute their disagreement to Bernoulli variation, annotator location, or both. The rows do not license assigning the predicate a categorical event type.

## Declaring what is outside the process

The original protocol uses the natural-parts answer to determine which later
questions appear. A yes reveals questions about part similarity and part duration;
a no reveals questions about whole-event duration and dynamicity. This display logic
matters, but the present extract does not contain branch responses whose raw fields
can be verified against the documented scales. Raw confidence is also blocked: the
paper describes a one-to-five scale, the package metadata describes a zero-to-four
scale, and the inspected raw serialization repeats a duration response in the
confidence position. The released normalized confidence field is thus not treated
as an additional raw judgment.

Thus this DGP generates the observed natural-parts gate responses. The full
instrument also displays conditional questions about similarity, duration, and
dynamicity, but their raw responses cannot be verified in this extract. Those
branches remain outside the likelihood, so the fitted parameters describe response
propensities for the gate under this protocol.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the generative order"}
1. Which quantity in the model is recorded directly?
2. Why do the rows for one item share $u_i$ but not $a_j$?
3. Why is an item identifier not a verb-lemma identifier?
4. Which response branches remain outside this model?

**Answers.** (1) Only $Y_{ij}$, along with its item and annotator identifiers, is recorded directly. (2) Rows for one predicate node share the same item deviation, while annotator IDs may differ. (3) The graph and node IDs anchor a predicate occurrence in context, so lemma identity alone does not determine the item. (4) Part similarity and part duration after yes, and dynamicity and event duration after no, remain outside the empirical gate model.
:::

A DGP orders the random choices and mappings that connect a linguistic target to an annotation. The next page translates this sequence into [one joint distribution](writing-a-joint-model.qmd).

## Recap

1. The recorded variable is a binary response to a context-anchored predicate-node prompt.
2. The DGP separates that response from its latent probability and from item and annotator deviations.
3. Bernoulli sampling, a logit link, normal exchangeable effects, additivity, and conditional independence are assumptions that require checks.
4. The [joint-factorization section](writing-a-joint-model.qmd#translating-steps-into-factors) next converts these steps into one probability expression without adding unobserved pairs.
